To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hotel industry in Hong Kong is undergoing significant changes in the wake of the economic crisis.
the HR practices in the hotel industry in Hong Kong are not flexible and do not foster creativity.
the economic downturn of 1997-1998 had a significant impact on Hong Kong's hotel industry.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the extent to which human resource management (HRM) practices can be adapted to meet the needs of a changing business environment and the extent to which the hotel industry can respond to the challenge of a changing business climate.
the extent to which organizations can respond to the demands of a turbulent business environment and how this is reflected in the management of human resources.
understanding how organizations respond to the challenge of economic uncertainty.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Hong Kong hotels are still in the midst of the economic crisis and the typhoon is far from over.
the HRM practices in this sector are in the process of change, and this is reflected by the fact that the majority of hotels have not yet adopted any formalized HRM practices.
the HR response to economic crisis in the hotel industry in Hong Kong is a combination of both the good and the not so good.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hotel industry in Hong Kong has been able to survive the typhoon, and even to prosper in some instances.
the crisis has had a profound effect on the hotel industry, and that managers have responded by attempting to balance flexibility with control, but with limited success.

, while there is a clear recognition of the need for flexibility, the cultural and structural factors that inhibit the development of such flexibility are deeply entrenched in the organization, and the ability of the organizations to develop a climate that would facilitate creativity and innovation is limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the crisis has not led to a fundamental re-thinking of the human resource management (HRM) approach in Hong Kong.
managers need to be more proactive in their efforts to create an innovative and creative environment.

, in order to be able to respond effectively to the economic downturn, managers should not be afraid to allow their employees to exercise a degree of autonomy and flexibility, and to be able to take initiative.
